In July, The Beach Boys drop the song "I Get Around" and snag the #1 spot.  ◻️ December 1965  The Beatles release the groundbreaking "Rubber Soul" album. Wilson is "so blown away" by it that he immediately goes in the studio, smokes a joint and writes "God Only Knows" (which Paul McCartney cites as his favourite song ever).  That song kicks off The Beach Boys next album.  ◻️May 1966  The Beach Boys finish the "Pet Sounds" album. It's writing, vocal harmonies, consistent theme and use of non-traditional instruments (French horns, sleigh bells) pushes the envelope.  They give McCartney and John Lennon an advance listen to the album.   McCartney recalls how “Pet Sounds” affected The Beatles: "That was the album that flipped me. The musical invention on that album was wow! I just thought, ‘Oh dear me. This is the album of our time. What the hell are we going to do?’"  ◻️August 1966  The Beatles release another classic album ("Revolver") with McCartney writing a few songs inspired by "God Only Knows".   ◻️ February 1967  The Beach Boys are working on their "Pet Sounds" follow-up album called "Smile".   The Beatles release the song "Strawberry Fields Forever". Wilson hears the song while driving and — years later — remembers his reaction: “I had to pull over to the side of the road…and I said, ‘I’ve never heard anything like this in my life’”. title: Unblocking: the small favor that builds a whole scene
summary:
It kicked off when @__drewface coined “unblocking” as the secret sauce of great creative clusters — and suddenly everyone had a word for the thing they wished their friends would do for them: notice your work, remove a snag, nudge you to ship. Drew didn’t pitch it as vibes; he stacked receipts (Oppenheimer prowling for stuck experiments, von Neumann rescuing “laughed out of the room” ideas, C.S. Lewis keeping Tolkien from shelving LOTR, Homebrew’s free-help culture) and then named the mechanics: “favor abundance” (asking for help *adds* status) and “baton race culture” (you run hard, then openly hand off blockers so the group can carry it).

The arc is basically: Visa’s long-running “build a scene” drumbeat → Drew’s thread makes it sticky → the friend-group proves it in real time. @visakanv had already been yelling since 2019 that “any small group… can create powerful vectors by producing public-facing work directed at each other,” plus the hard-edged filter: “sad thing is… few people have any real creative vision,” followed by his own mellowing self-myth (“2007: fuck everyone… 2019: there is no fuck”). Then the meta-peak: @Malcolm_Ocean reveals the actual unblocking chain — Visa tells Malcolm “a flourishing scene is… people unblock each other at a tremendous rate,” Malcolm threatens to tweet it, which pushes Visa to push Drew to publish the thread. Everyone’s like “very meta,” but it’s also the point: scenius isn’t a theory, it’s an *intervention loop*.

After that, it stops being a cute concept and turns into tooling. @tasshinfogleman basically heckles them into operationalizing it (“explain… standing on one foot”), and @visakanv responds with a dead-simple 5-step protocol: write what you want, write what’s stopping you, share both, encourage others to do it, repeat. @rickbenger extends it into the physical world with “Colliders” (spaces that hold diverse people + practices without collapsing) and explicitly calls out “an ‘unblocking’ cascade” as the felt effect. By 2024 it’s canon (“unblocking is now a core word to me,” says @AskYatharth; Tasshin lists “unblock the people you care about” as Threadapalooza wisdom), and by 2025 @DefenderOfBasic is trying to automate the whole thing with a “semantic engine” that streams frontier work and connects people “in latent space,” while also pushing new shareable formats (image-essays, numbered “editions”) as distribution infrastructure.

Why care: this thread cluster is basically a DIY blueprint for turning “I have talented friends” into “we ship like a machine.” The residue is vocabulary you can actually use on Tuesday (“I’m blocked,” “can you unblock me?” “favor abundance,” “collider”) and a norm shift: asking for help isn’t cringe, it’s how scenes manufacture momentum.
